full_judgment:
2. Plaintiffs instituted a suit being OC Suit No. 145 of 1983 in the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Pabna against the Government praying for declaration of their title to certain lands described in the schedule of the plaint. Pursuant to the summons, the defendant appeared in the suit but did not file any written statement. The suit was, however, decreed ex-parte on 22-12-1983. Thereafter, the defendant appears to have filed an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting-aside the ex-parte decree. The application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 14 of 1984. As no step was taken by the defendant on 19-5-1984, the date fixed for hearing of the matter, the case was dismissed for default. The defendant did not prefer any appeal therefrom but filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the Miscellaneous Case alleging, inter alia, that the Moharar of the Government took note in his diary that the matter was fixed for hearing on 17-5-1984 but since that date the record of the case could not be traced in spite of the best efforts of the defendant and that the Government would suffer an irreparable loss if the case be not restored to its file and number. The plaintiffs did not file any written objection thereto. The learned sub-ordinate Judge after hearing the parties found that the defendant failed to appear on the date of hearing owing to the mistake of the Bench Clerk. Accordingly he passed the impugned order dated 19-7-1984 restoring the Miscellaneous Case. Against the said order the plaintiffs have obtained this Rule from this Court. 

 3. Mr. MA Mannan, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner first, submits that the order dated 19-5-1984 dismissing the Miscellaneous Case No. 14 of 1984 was appeal-able under Order XLIII, rule 1(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure and, as such, there being an alternative remedy by way of appeal the application under section 151 of the Code before the learned Sub-ordinate Judge was not maintain-able. He next submits that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge committed an error of law in holding that the defendant could not appear on the date of the hearing of the Miscellaneous Case owing to the mistake of the Bench Clerk of the Court inasmuch as, the learned Sub-ordinate Judge failed to notice that 17-5-1984 and 18-5-1984 being closed holidays there was an obligation on the part of the defendant to appear on 19-5-84 on which date the Court reopened and the matter was taken up for disposal. 

 5. According to the learned Advocate for the petitioner, the finding of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge that the default of the defendant in appearance at the hearing of the case was due to the mistake of the Bench Clerk is erroneous in that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge has failed to notice hat 17-5-84 which was the date fixed for hearing as per the alleged noting in the diary of the Government Moharar was declared a holiday and it was, therefore, the duty of the defendant to be present on 19-5-84 when the Court was reopened but the defendant defaulted. So the learned Advocate submits that the failure of the defendant to appear on 19-5-84 was not due to the mistake of the Bench Clerk but due to the negligence of the defendant. It transpires that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge examined the materials on record, particularly the Cause list of the Court and upon consideration of the same found that 17-5-84 was wrongly shown as the date fixed for hearing of the Miscellaneous Case in the Cause list owing to the mistake of the Bench Clerk although the matter was fixed for hearing on 19-5-84. This finding is essentially as finding of fact which could not be challenged by the learned Advocate. It is true that 17-5-84 was declared a holiday and 18-5-84 being Friday was a weekly holiday and the Court remained closed on both the days. On 19-5-84 the Court was re-opened, but the defendant did not appear. The pertinent question that arises, therefore, is whether the defendant had any legal obligation to appear on the re-opening of the Court, if to his knowledge the hearing was fixed on a date which was closed for a holiday. Although the learned Advocate has submitted that the defendant had an obligation to be present on the re-opening he could not point out any provision of law or cite any decision in support of his submission. 

 6. The learned Deputy Attorney-General has contended that the defendant had no legal duty to appear on the next day if the Court remained closed on the date fixed for hearing. The learned Deputy Attorney-General cited the case of Md Swaleh vs M/S United Grain & Fodder Agencies, (1964) 16 DLR (SC), 155 in support of his submission. In that case the trial court fixed 21st April, 1960 for recording evidence but the day was subsequently declared a closed holiday. The file was taken up by the Court on the next day i.e. 22nd April, 1960 when the plaintiffs was present but the defendants were absent. The Court passed an order for ex-parte disposal and fixed 27-4-1960 for proof and order. On 27th April, 1960 as nobody appeared for the defendants the suit was decreed ex-parte. The defendant then filed application u/s 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying that the ex-parte decree as well as the order dated 22-4-1960 directing ex-parte proceeding be set-aside The application having been allowed by the Sub-ordinate Judge the High Court of West Pakistan was moved against the said order and a Single Judge of the High Court set-aside the order upon the view, inter alia, that it was the duty of a litigant to appear on the next day if the court remained closed on the date fixed for hearing. Upon and appeal therefrom, the Supreme Court of Pakistan found no basis for the view and accordingly set-aside the order of the High Court. 

 7. Reference may also be made to Mt Umat-ul-Mughim Begum vs Salig Rain, AIR, 1915 Lah 476, Raghumandan Lohar vs Bachu Singh, 1940 Pat, 475 Punj 80 in this respect. We respectfully concur with the view expressed in the said decisions. In the absence of any specific provision of law requiring a party to be present on the following day where the date fixed for hearing a case happens to be a holiday, we are of the opinion that a failure of a party to appear on the re-opening of the Court in a case like the present one does not amount to negligence. 

 8. Now let us consider the submission as to the application of section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of a proceeding under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code dis. missed for default. It is strenuously urged by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the inherent power of the Court contemplated in section 151 of the Code cannot be invoked in a care covered by a specific provision in the Code or where there is an alternative remedy. He cited the case of Azizur Rahman vs Janata Bank, (1976) 28 DLR 252 in support of his submission. According to him, in the instant case there being an alternative remedy by way of appeal under Order XLIII, rule 1(d) of the Code, the learned Sub-ordinate Judge had no jurisdiction to invoke inherent power under section 151 of the Code for restoration of the Miscellaneous Case dismissed for default. 

 9. It is now well-settled that powers under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure are not to be invoked where there is specific provision in the Code which covers a patrician case or if there is a positive prohibition against an act or there is an alternative remedy, but in a series of judicial decisions it has been pointed out that this general rule is subject to an important exception in that where a mistake of a Court or Court's Officer causes some injustice to a party, the power under section 151 of the Code can be exercised for the purpose of doing justice, even though such an act is prohibited under the general law or there is an alternative remedy for doing the same. It is cardinal principle that an act of Court shall prejudice none. It would he unjust to penalise a party for a mistake which was essentially of the Court. It will be pertinent to refer here to the following observations of their Lordships in the case of Punjab Ali Pramanik vs Md. Mokarram Hossain 29 DLR (SC) 185 :— 

 "It appears to us that the preponderant judicial view which emerges out of the authorities referred to above and with which we find ourselves in agreement is that the Court should not presume the existence of inherent power to do that for which specific provision has been made by a statute and should not invest such jurisdiction for the purpose of getting round the express provisions of the law. Unintentional or inadvertent mistake a Court causing some injustice to a party, however, stands on a different footing and in the case of such a mistake, the exercise of inherent power of a Court is not subject to these limitations on its exercise which have been set down by the judicial authorities noticed above." 

 10. The principle of law indicated in the above case applies in full force to the facts of the present case In view of the fact as found by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge that due to the mistake of Bench Clerk the defendant failed to appear on the date of hearing of the Miscellaneous Case, we are of the view that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge was right in invoking inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the Miscellaneous Case. 

 11. The jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is a discretionary one. It is to be exercised where it is called for in the ends of justice and not otherwise. Regard being had to the facts and circumstances of the case we do not find any error in the impugned order which has occasioned a failure of justice in the case.
